section.title: Constant velocity: where slope and area first meet
section.p: The dashboard gave us two questions. Constant velocity is the first case where both questions can be answered without any limiting process.

hint.p: A constant rate means equal distance in equal time. What kind of graph has a constant slope?

exercise.title: Why are slope and area inverse clues?

statement.p: From the distance graph we read velocity as a slope; from the velocity graph we read distance as an area. In your own words, why are those two readings inverse operations rather than two unrelated pictures?

hint.p: One process extracts a rate from an accumulated quantity. The other process rebuilds the accumulated quantity from the rate.

subsection.title: Why the word “constant” matters
subsection.p: The formula

The average velocity over the full hour is 50 miles/hour, but the car was never moving at 50 miles/hour during either half of the trip.
The velocity graph is no longer one horizontal line. It has two steps. The distance graph is no longer one straight line. It has two line segments, one with slope 30 and one with slope 70.

figure.caption: When velocity changes by steps, distance is built from several straight pieces. Each piece has its own slope.

subsection.p: This example is still simple because the velocity is constant on each half-hour piece. We can add two rectangle areas.
But real motion rarely changes only once. A driver speeds up, slows down, stops, and starts again. The velocity graph may have many pieces, or no flat pieces at all.
The next step is to allow motion forward and backward. Then area below the time axis must count with a sign. That sign is not a technicality; it is how calculus remembers direction.

exercise.title: What does the word constant buy us?

statement.p: The exact slope-and-area story in this section used a velocity that never changed. In your own words, what would break if the velocity started changing while the clock was running, and what new idea will be needed?

hint.p: Rectangles and a single slope are exact only when the height of the velocity graph does not move. Changing height forces smaller pieces, then a limiting process.
